::: {.lead}
In this course you looked at a game from many sides: the hardware it runs
on, the operating systems, the platforms and their stores, the network and
the cloud, the test devices and the performance. The **project** puts these
sides together for **one game of your choice**: a short **platform report**
and a **five-minute presentation**. Lina, a student, chose the puzzle game
*Tile Garden* and asked: "PC or console next?" In this seminar you finish
your report, build six clear slides, rehearse the talk, and check your work
against the rubric. You work alone. Each section is one step of the seminar
and ends with a task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary project-brief presentation-rubric reliable-source comparison-criteria decision-matrix system-requirements test-environment compatibility-matrix >}}

## 28.1 Step 1: the project report

The report has six parts (@fig-parts).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 28.1 — The project brief"}
**Task:** a platform report for one game (a real game or your own idea),
2–3 pages, individual.

1. **The game:** genre, players, controls, the question of the report.
2. **Platforms:** two platforms compared with criteria (lectures 15, 23,
   24).
3. **Specs:** targets and system requirements (lectures 5–8, 24).
4. **Test plan:** emulators, real devices, a device matrix (lectures
   25–26).
5. **Risks:** performance and compatibility, with fixes (lecture 27).
6. **Publishing:** store rules and cloud services (lectures 17–22).

Every fact has a **reliable source with a date**. Your teacher gives the
deadline and the final rubric on the e-learning platform.
:::

![The six parts of the report.](images/project-parts.png){#fig-parts width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 28.1 — Lina's plan"}
1. *Game:* *Tile Garden*, a calm puzzle game for phones, 5-minute sessions.
2. *Question:* PC or console as the next platform?
3. *Sources:* the store pages and developer documentation of both
   platforms, a dated market report, and Lina's own tests in an emulator.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Choosing a game that is too big ("an open-world game on all platforms").
A small game and one clear question make a better report.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your project plan"}
Write your game, your question and three sources you will use (name and
date).

*Your result:* a five-line plan.
:::

## 28.2 Step 2: six slides

A five-minute talk needs about six slides (@fig-slides).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 28.2 — Six slides"}
1. The game and the question.
2. The two platforms compared (a table or a decision matrix).
3. Specs and targets.
4. The test plan.
5. Risks and fixes.
6. The recommendation: the answer to the question.

One message per slide, written as a short sentence in the title; numbers
with their source; text large enough to read (24 pt or more).
:::

![Six slides, five minutes.](images/slide-structure.png){#fig-slides width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 28.2 — Lina's slide titles"}
1. "Tile Garden on PC or console? The question of this report."
2. "Two platforms compared: reach, cost, controls, testing."
3. "Specs and targets: 60 fps on a weak PC, 4K on the console."
4. "Test plan: two emulators, one weak laptop, a device farm."
5. "Risks and fixes: many PC configurations, certification."
6. "Recommendation: PC first (37 of 50), console next year."
:::

{{< sim file="sims/slide-sorter.html" poster="sims/slide-sorter.png" title="Slide Sorter: a five-minute talk" height="580" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Slides full of text read aloud. The slide shows the message and the
number; you say the rest.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your slide titles"}
1. In **Slide Sorter**, put Lina's slides in order.
2. Write the six slide titles of your own talk as short sentences.

*Your result:* six titles.
:::

## 28.3 Step 3: presenting and answering

A good talk is practised (@fig-slides).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 28.3 — The talk"}
- **Time:** about 50 seconds per slide; practise with a timer.
- **Voice:** speak to the audience, not to the screen; pause after the
  important numbers.
- **Questions:** answer with facts from your report. If you do not know,
  say so and offer to check the source. Never invent a number.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 28.3 — A hard question"}
1. The teacher asks Lina: "How many players use the console in your
   country?"
2. Lina has no number for the country and says: "My source gives only
   worldwide numbers from last year; I will check a local report."
3. Honest, short, and it shows that Lina knows the sources.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Speeding up to fit too much into five minutes. Cut words and side topics,
not the question, the numbers or the answer.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Rehearse"}
Present your six slides alone with a timer. Write the time, and three
questions the audience may ask, with short answers.

*Your result:* a time and three questions with answers.
:::

## 28.4 Step 4: check before you present

Check your work against the rubric (@fig-rubric).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 28.4 — The rubric"}
A **presentation rubric** lists the criteria and the marks. In the example
rubric: content 4, sources 2, slides 2, talk 1, questions 1 (10 marks).
Check each criterion honestly, fix the weakest one first, and practise
again.
:::

![An example rubric.](images/rubric.png){#fig-rubric width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 28.4 — Lina's self-check"}
1. Content: six parts, checked facts: yes. Sources: two numbers without a
   date: partly.
2. Slides: slide 3 is crowded: partly. Talk: 5 min 20 s: yes.
3. Lina adds the dates and splits slide 3. Expected marks rise from 8 to
   10.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/project-check.html" poster="sims/project-check.png" title="Project Check: before you hand in" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Checking only the slides. The report, the sources and the answers to
questions are marked too.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Self-check"}
In **Project Check**, answer the six questions for your project, then fix
the two items that give the most marks.

*Your result:* an expected mark and two fixes.
:::

## Case study: Talk Doctor

Six students rehearse their talks: a crowded slide read aloud, an
11-minute talk, a number without a source, a chart without axis names, a
question without an answer, and a talk that ends without the
recommendation. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
rehearsals. In the mini-game below you choose the best advice for each
one.

## Further reading

Reynolds, *Presentation Zen* (3rd ed., 2019), on simple slides. Duarte,
*Slide:ology* (2008), the chapters on one message per slide and on charts.

## Exercises

1. Name the six parts of the project report.
2. Why should the game and the question be small?
3. What must every fact in the report have?
4. Name the six slides of the talk.
5. How long should each slide take in a five-minute talk?
6. What makes a good slide title?
7. What do you do when you cannot answer a question?
8. What is a presentation rubric?
9. Which criterion should you fix first?
10. Why practise with a timer?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. The game, platforms, specs, test plan, risks, publishing.
2. So that one clear question can be answered well in the report.
3. A reliable source with a date.
4. The game and the question, the platforms compared, specs and targets,
   the test plan, risks and fixes, the recommendation.
5. About 50 seconds.
6. One message as a short sentence.
7. Say so honestly and offer to check the source.
8. A table of criteria and marks for the presentation.
9. The weakest one that gives the most marks.
10. To keep to five minutes without cutting the important parts.
:::
